title: The dove and the olive leaf (Genesis 8:6–12)
hook: the raven doesn't return; the dove comes back with a leaf

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flood: creation run backwards, and the turn when God remembered Noah. Your line: god remembers.

Before radar and satellites, sailors lost at sea sometimes carried birds on board. When they couldn't see land, they'd let one go and watch. If it circled and came back, there was no shore within reach. If it flew off in a straight line, they followed it. The ark has been floating for months. The rain has stopped, the waters are going down, and the box has come to rest on the mountains of Ararat. But there's one window, and all Noah can see through it is sky. So he does what those sailors did, and lets a bird go.
screen: `SAILORS LOST AT SEA, A BIRD ON BOARD.` → `THE ARK RESTS ON ARARAT.` → `NOAH OPENS THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: The first bird is a raven. In the King James Bible, it "went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth." It never comes back with news. Ravens can live on what they find, even in a drowned world. Then Noah sends a dove. She finds nowhere to rest her foot, and comes back. And there's a tender detail here: Noah puts out his hand, and takes her, and pulls her in. A man who hasn't said a word in the whole story, reaching out the window for a tired bird. He waits seven days. He sends her again. And this time: "And the dove came in to him in the evening; and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated from off the earth." One leaf. Not a field, not dry ground under his feet. Just a single fresh leaf in a bird's beak. Olive trees are tough; they can come back from almost nothing. And that leaf is enough for Noah to know. Something is growing again out there. He waits seven more days, sends her one last time, and she doesn't come back at all. Which is good news too: she's found a home. In Hebrew, dove is yonah, the same as the prophet Jonah's name. And for Christians, the dove will return at the Jordan River, when the Spirit comes down on Jesus at his baptism like a dove. Centuries later, the dove with an olive branch became a picture of peace across the world. It started with one leaf at evening.
screen: `THE RAVEN GOES TO AND FRO.` · `NOAH PULLS THE DOVE IN.` · `ONE OLIVE LEAF.` · `YONAH: THE DOVE FOUND A HOME.` · then, large: `IN HER MOUTH WAS AN OLIVE LEAF.`

segments.voice: Think about the part of your life that still feels underwater, and don't look for dry land or the whole answer; look for a leaf. One small thing growing again: a better morning, a kind word, a bill paid, one honest conversation. If you pray, you can give thanks for it.
Yonah. The Hebrew word for dove, the same as the prophet Jonah's name: the bird that came back with one green leaf.
Your line: a leaf is enough. The whole thing doesn't have to be fixed yet. That's day three hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: The dove appears across Christian art as a sign of the Holy Spirit and of peace, and in the catacombs of Rome early Christians drew a dove with an olive branch on tombs.

chat.says: Why did one olive leaf matter so much to Noah?
options: It showed the waters were going down and something was growing again.
It meant the land was dry, so Noah could leave the ark that same day.
It proved the raven had found land first, so the dove could follow.
chat.meaning: In her mouth was an olive leaf, so Noah knew the waters were abated. One fresh leaf was enough to know something was growing again.

notes: Sailors releasing birds to find land: an ancient practice (also in Mesopotamian flood stories and Pliny's account of Indian sailors). Stated generally; confirm.
'There's one window' (8:6) and 'all he can see through it is sky' is narrative inference; confirm acceptable.
Olive trees regrowing from roots/stumps is general botany; stated as 'can come back from almost nothing'. Confirm.
Doves with olive branches in Roman catacomb art (howItsDone); confirm.
'Noah hasn't said a word in the whole story' consistent with day 343. Confirm.
